title: Signs in the horizons and in themselves
hook: We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves (41:53)
carry: signs out there, signs in here

segments.voice: Yesterday, standing firm, istiqamah, and your line was say it, then stand firm. Did you keep your one small practice, even without feeling it? Day five hundred sixty-six.

Stand at the edge of a wide view, a coastline, a desert, a city at night from a high window, and you can feel yourself get small. Now close your eyes and feel your heartbeat, the breath going in and out without your asking, the strange fact that you're aware of any of it. That gets large in a different way. Two directions to look: out, as far as the eye goes, and in, as deep as you can go. Near its close, one verse before the last, Surah Fussilat points both ways at once.

Verse fifty-three. Pickthall: "We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves until it will be manifest unto them that it is the Truth." Portents, in Pickthall's English, is the Arabic ayat, signs. And ayat is also the word for the verses of the Qur'an. A verse is a sign. A sunset is a sign. Your own heartbeat is a sign. The same word covers all three. Then the two places. Al-afaq, the horizons: the far edges of the world, everything out there. And anfusihim, themselves: the inner world, the body, the mind, the soul. The verse says the signs will keep being shown, in both directions, until it becomes clear that this is the truth. What exactly are these signs? Commentators differ. Some early scholars read the horizons as the lands that would open to the Muslims and the selves as events in Mecca itself: history as a sign. Many later scholars read it as the cosmos and the human being: nature as a sign. The verse holds both. And Surah adh-Dhariyat says something similar: in the earth are signs for the certain, and in yourselves; do you not see? The verse ends with a question: isn't it enough that your Lord is witness over everything? So the signs aren't a puzzle to be solved once. They're shown, again and again, to anyone looking. Out at the horizon, in at the heartbeat, and down at the page.

The practice: look outside, then inside. If you can, look out a window, or step outside. Find the farthest thing you can see, a tree line, a rooftop, a cloud. Rest your eyes on it for a few breaths. Then close your eyes, and turn the looking inward. Feel your breath, your heartbeat, the fact that you're noticing at all. Move between the two, slowly, out and in. The bell holds the time.
Ayat, signs, the word that names both the Qur'an's verses and the proofs shown out at the world's horizons and within the self. Today's word.
Your line: signs out there, signs in here. Today, catch one sign out there, a sky, a tree, a stranger's kindness, and one in here, a breath, a feeling, a thought. Day five hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims practice tafakkur, reflection on creation and on the self, as a form of worship, and use the same word, ayah, for a verse of the Qur'an and a sign in the world.

what it means: signs are shown both out at the horizon and within the self, again and again, until the truth is clear.
what a scholar hears: ayat covers both scripture and creation; early tafsir read al-afaq as conquests and anfus as Mecca, later tafsir as cosmos and body; compare 51:20–21.
